newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Embassies advise nationals to avoid Cambodian rallies.
newsitem.headline: Embassies advise nationals to avoid Cambodian rallies.

text.p: Several embassies are advising their nationals to avoid political gatherings in Cambodia following a deadly grenade attack on an opposition rally in the capital last month, diplomats said on Friday.
"Violence has occurred at political rallies in Phnom Penh,and residents and visitors should avoid such events," said an Australian consular travel advice notice updated on April 8.

A British diplomat said the embassy had sent an update for their travel advisory to the Foreign Office in London on Friday. "We added an extra line advising tourists, visitors to beware of joining crowds at political rallies," he told Reuters.

Officials at the German and U.S. Embassies said they had also started warning nationals to avoid political gatherings and demonstrations following the March 30 grenade attack on an opposition Khmer Nation Party demonstration.
The blasts left up to 19 people dead and more than 100 injured in the deadliest single act of political violence in the country in years.
Barnaby Jones, aid worker and security advisor to foreign non-governmental organisations in Cambodia, said he had advised people to avoid crowded, public areas following the grenade attack.
But some embassies, including those of France, Thailand and Malaysia, said they were not amending their advice to their nationals visiting or living in Cambodia.

"I'm confident that nothing's going to happen. We are not going to issue any advisory notes to any of the Malaysians here-- most of them are quite seasoned," Malaysian Ambassador to Cambodia Kamal Ismaun told Reuters.

The March 30 attack increased tensions between the two main parties in the coalition formed after U.N.-run elections in 1993 and some analysts feared the tragedy could herald a campaign of violence ahead of general elections due next year.

Sam Rainsy earlier this year formed an alliance with the royalist FUNCINPEC party of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, which rules in uneasy partnership with Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party.
